clue.text: Difficulty for leaders of BBC Lineker epitomised, maybe

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their first letters, taken from each of the four words that follow

explanation.surface: A spot of bother at the BBC, perhaps involving its football presenter Gary Lineker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' gives PRO in the sense of being in favour; 'maybe' is not a question-marker here but the fourth word whose leader is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: A problem is a difficulty, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Eat in the open air breeze

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to have a meal outdoors

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an outdoor meal on a breezy day; breeze is the informal word for an easy task.
explanation.definitionFit: Picnic is both an outdoor meal and, informally, a task that is easy to do.

clue.text: Live in old vessel in outskirts of city

indicators.note: in places the vessel inside the city's edge letters
the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: a cup is a drinking vessel

explanation.surface: Someone lives in an old ship moored on the edge of a city.
explanation.definitionFit: To occupy a house is to live in it or inhabit it.

clue.text: What Napoleon showed the French before he'd Paris reconstructed

indicators.note: before puts the French article ahead of the rest

parts.note: le is the French word for 'the'

indicators.note: reconstructed says the letters are rebuilt into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Napoleon displayed command before rebuilding Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in he'd is ignored, so its letters join Paris in the rearranging. The definition works because Napoleon was a commander.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon commanded armies and an empire, showing the quality of leading others.

clue.text: Bumps into this writer and gets head scratched

parts.note: the setter refers to themself, giving me

indicators.note: scratching the head of a word strikes out its first letter

explanation.surface: The writer collides with something and ends up scratching his head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head scratched' reads as a puzzled gesture but tells you to strike the first letter of gets.
explanation.definitionFit: To meet someone by chance is to bump into them.

clue.text: Boats — some cross less evasively on the way back

indicators.note: on the way back says the hidden letters are read in reverse order
some of the words says only part of their letters is used

explanation.surface: Boats crossing a stretch of water head home, steering less evasively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' picks SLESSEV out of 'cross less evasively', and 'on the way back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Vessels are ships or boats, craft that travel on water.

clue.text: Moral weakness reduced Conservatives' wins

indicators.note: reduced says the word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a vice is a moral failing or weakness
Tories are members of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Moral failings have cut down the Conservatives' election wins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' cuts VICE to VIC; Tories are Britain's Conservatives.
explanation.definitionFit: Victories are successes or triumphs in a contest.

clue.text: Type of music only on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio says the word is heard rather than seen, so it is replaced by one sounding the same

parts.note: sole means only, single

explanation.surface: A kind of music played only on the radio.
explanation.definitionFit: Soul is a genre of African-American popular music rooted in gospel and rhythm and blues.

clue.text: Allowed goal, securing championship

indicators.note: securing says the first word holds the second within it

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal
a title is a championship won in sport

explanation.surface: A football goal is allowed, clinching the championship.
explanation.definitionFit: Entitled means having the right to something, so permitted.

clue.text: Might get thorns out with nothing missing

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are put out of order
missing says the letter for nothing is taken from the pool before rearranging

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Gardening advice: you might pull the thorns out and leave nothing behind.
explanation.walkthrough: Take O away from GETTHORNS and 'out' rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Might as a noun means power or force, the same as strength.

clue.text: Caught Oscar twice with a drink

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
O is Oscar in the NATO phonetic alphabet
twice says caught and Oscar are given a second time, so the same two letters come again; with just joins on the A

explanation.surface: Someone named Oscar is caught out twice, with a drink in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocoa is a hot chocolate drink made from powdered cacao beans.

clue.text: English knight opposing battle

parts.note: N is the chess notation for a knight
counter means opposing, contrary

explanation.surface: An English knight faces his opponent in battle.
explanation.definitionFit: An encounter is a clash or fight between opposing forces.

clue.text: Hollow feeling

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a dent or depression left by pressing
second meaning: a vague sense or notion about something

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a hollow, empty feeling, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: An impression is both a mark pressed into a surface and an idea or sense one forms.

clue.text: Shake second barrel

parts.note: a tun is a large cask or barrel

explanation.surface: Instructions for mixing a drink: shake, then a second barrel.
explanation.definitionFit: To stun someone is to shock or daze them, as a piece of news can shake them.

clue.text: Having a talk about Alice's mad acquaintance in golf

parts.note: C stands for circa, Latin for about
the Mad Hatter, whom Alice meets in Alice in Wonderland
G is golf in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone chats about the Mad Hatter while out on a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: Chattering means talking quickly and continuously, holding a conversation.

clue.text: Struggling in maths set? No wonder

indicators.note: struggling suggests letters thrashing about, so these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pupil struggling in a maths set: no wonder, perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Astonishment is great surprise or amazement, as is wonder.

clue.text: Running record brought up in speech

indicators.note: in puts the reversed record inside the speech

parts.note: an oration is a formal speech

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means read from bottom to top, so reversed

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A record of running is mentioned in a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The operation of a machine is its running or working.

clue.text: Brave before prison sentence makes you quail?

indicators.note: before puts this ahead of the next piece

parts.note: game means plucky or brave, willing
bird is British slang for a jail term, from rhyming slang bird-lime for time

explanation.surface: Faced with jail, even a brave person may quail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quail' looks like the verb to cower, but it is the bird, an example hence the question mark. Bird is British slang for a spell in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A quail is a small bird shot for sport, an example of a game bird.

clue.text: Small lingerie covering right bits

indicators.note: covering says the underwear goes round the next letter

parts.note: undies is an informal word for underwear

explanation.surface: Skimpy underwear that barely covers the right bits.
explanation.definitionFit: Sundries are miscellaneous small items, odds and ends.

clue.text: A trusty vine I scrambled up

indicators.note: scrambled says the letters are mixed up into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone recalls scrambling up a sturdy vine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' is the British sense of being in residence at a university, as in going up to Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a student who is up is in residence at college, especially Oxford or Cambridge.

clue.text: Editor upset with blunt argument

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so read backwards

parts.note: to bate is to lessen or blunt, as in abate

explanation.surface: An editor is upset by a blunt row.
explanation.definitionFit: A debate is a formal discussion in which opposing views are put forward.

clue.text: Witness most portly female getting abandoned

indicators.note: getting abandoned says this letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: fattest means most portly

explanation.surface: The stoutest woman, left on her own, gives evidence.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest is to bear witness, to declare something is true.

clue.text: Finishes repairs with month to go

indicators.note: to go says this letter is to leave the word, so it is removed

parts.note: mends means repairs

explanation.surface: Repair work finishes with a month still remaining.
explanation.definitionFit: Ends as a verb means finishes or concludes.

clue.text: Command soldiers wearing magenta pants

indicators.note: wearing puts the soldiers inside, the anagram worn around them
pants is British slang for rubbish, so the word magenta is a bad version, rearranged

parts.note: men is a common term for soldiers

explanation.surface: An order for soldiers to wear magenta trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' (British slang for rubbish) rearranges magenta to MANAGET, and 'wearing' puts MEN inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Management is control or direction of an organisation, a sense of command.

clue.text: Makes fun of topless relatives

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, so it is removed

parts.note: taunts means makes fun of

explanation.surface: Mocking relatives who go topless.
explanation.definitionFit: Aunts are family members, sisters of one's parents.

clue.text: Friendly with a Republican male

explanation.surface: Getting on well with a Republican man.
explanation.definitionFit: A warm welcome is a friendly, cordial one.

clue.text: Mock student leaving bar

indicators.note: leaving says this letter goes out of the word

parts.note: a limitation is a restriction or bar
L is a learner driver's plate, used for a student

explanation.surface: Students jeer at a classmate who walks out of the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' removes L, the learner plate standing for a student, from LIMITATION.
explanation.definitionFit: Mock as an adjective means fake or imitation, as in mock leather.

clue.text: Complain an election's somewhat foolish

indicators.note: somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Grumbling about an election is rather foolish.
explanation.definitionFit: Inane means silly or senseless, lacking sense.

clue.text: Polish chap's rubbish job

parts.note: to dust is to clean or polish furniture
man means a chap; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A Polish man complains that his job is rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like a nationality but is the verb to polish. The definition is cryptic: this worker's job is literally rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A dustman, in Britain, collects household refuse, so his work is all about rubbish.

clue.text: Show excited guests around centre of Bangkok

indicators.note: around says the shuffled letters go round the next piece
excited means stirred up, so the letters of guests are put into a new order
the centre of a seven-letter word is its fourth letter

explanation.surface: A tour guide shows excited visitors around central Bangkok.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' turns guests into SUGEST, which goes 'around' G, the centre of Bangkok.
explanation.definitionFit: To suggest something is to indicate or point to it, a sense of show.
